subject: Cash purchase vs leveraged — when each one actually wins
preheader: No-debt cash flow vs leveraged compounding · The 'one good deal' problem with all-cash

marketSnapshot.headline: Cash buy vs financed: different math, different answer
marketSnapshot.body: Some investors buy rental properties in cash. Most use leverage. There's no universal right answer — they optimize for different things. Cash buying maximizes monthly cash flow per property and minimizes risk; leverage maximizes returns on capital and lets you control more property with the same dollars. The decision depends on your capital base, risk tolerance, and what you're optimizing for. The math is more interesting than people think.

dealSpotter.address: Example: cash buy of a single property
dealSpotter.body: Single SFR purchased cash. Annual NCF $16,800. CoC 8.4% on the $200k deployed. Zero mortgage risk, no DSCR constraint, no foreclosure risk if vacancy hits. The downside: $200k is all in one property in one zip code. Diversification = zero. If that one property faces a major issue (foundation, fire, prolonged vacancy), you have no other income from that capital.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: 4 SFRs at 25% down · $2,200 NCF/mo combined · CoC 13.2%
dealSpotter.body: Same $200k as down payments on 4 separate $200k properties (25% down each). Total combined NCF $2,200/mo. CoC 13.2% on the same capital. Plus: 4 properties of principal paydown, 4 properties of appreciation exposure, geographic diversification. Downside: 4 mortgages, 4 DSCR constraints, 4 risks of rate-driven margin compression.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: 1 cash property + 1 leveraged · balanced risk + return
dealSpotter.body: $200k = one $200k cash property + $100k down on a $400k leveraged property. Combined NCF $2,100/mo. The cash property provides anchor stability (no mortgage, no rate risk). The leveraged property provides growth + compounding. Most thoughtful investors end up here over time — a mix that hedges different risks.

blogFeature.title: Cash-on-cash vs IRR — what each tells you about a deal
blogFeature.excerpt: Cash-on-cash is the metric cash buyers love. IRR is what leveraged investors should optimize for. Two different metrics that answer two different questions about the same deal.

qa.question: I have $300k available. Should I buy one property cash or three properties leveraged?
qa.answer: Depends on your goals and risk tolerance. The all-cash play gives you $300k in one property generating ~$2,000-2,500/mo of stable rental income with zero financing risk. The 3-property leveraged play gives you ~$3,500-5,000/mo of combined rental income across three properties with three mortgages, three sets of tenant risk, but also three properties of equity build. The math favor leverage when interest rates are below your cap rates (positive leverage), and unwinds when rates are above your cap rates (negative leverage). At today's rates (mortgages roughly 6-7%, cap rates 6-8% in solid markets), leverage is marginally positive — not the obvious win it was in 2018-2021. The risk-adjusted answer for most investors with $300k: 2 properties leveraged at moderate LTV (60-70%, not maxed at 75-80%). This captures most of the leverage upside while keeping each property cash-flow-strong enough to weather setbacks.
